title: Celebrating the Craft of Audio Description on ‘Happy Gilmore 2’ and ‘Stranger Things’ Season 5
summary: Netflix is recognized for both People’s Choice audio description awards for Happy Gilmore 2 and Stranger Things.
body_markdown:
Listen to the audio version of this article below.


At Netflix, we want to entertain the world, and that ambition is strengthened by our belief that entertainment is for everyone.


Yesterday, the Audio Description Awards Gala's People's Choice Awards recognized Netflix for Best Audio Description in two categories:


Happy Gilmore 2


(Film) and


Stranger Things


Season 5 (Series). We want to thank the American Council of the Blind for this incredible recognition, and the teams at Netflix, Descriptive Video Works (DVW), and International Digital Centre (IDC) who earned it.


Audio description (AD) is a creative craft. Every choice, from what to describe to how to say it, shapes how blind and low-vision members experience a story. DVW and IDC’s writers and narrators have worked alongside our Content Localization team for years to build that craft across our catalog, matching tone and timing scene by scene so every member can experience the story the way it’s meant to be felt.


Happy Gilmore 2


is a slapstick comedy, which makes accurate and engaging AD central to the creative intent. The description has to keep pace with the jokes and land the


[visual gags](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=q9yH3jxVKLc) so our blind and low-vision members laugh at the right moment.


“This can be really tricky with physical comedy because there's often dialogue going on at the same time, which interferes with our ability to put the description where we'd want to,” said Melissa Hope, Client Services Manager at DVW. “There's also the challenge of describing the joke in a way that's funny, and making sure we don't over-describe it in a way that might feel like we're explaining the joke instead of revealing the joke.”


Maddy Fenton, Project Manager at DVW, built the team with that challenge in mind. The narrator, Justin Smallbridge, was cast as a soundalike to the original film's AD narrator, carrying forward a voice audiences already associate with the franchise, and Erin Muroski, an award-winning comedy writer, was chosen for her experience bringing audiences into physical humor without flattening the joke.


After the AD was recorded, Anton A. Hill, a quality-control specialist who identifies as visually impaired, reviewed the script, narration, and final mix, and the team recorded several pickups for changes and added lines based on his notes. AD for


Happy Gilmore 2


was available in 14 languages on the day it premiered.


Creating the AD for


Stranger Things


meant capturing its suspenseful atmosphere, from the dread of a flashlight beam cutting through the dark to a look between characters that carries as much weight as the line that follows. That attention to detail mattered down to the word choice. Season 5 includes a scene set during Season 1 that audiences never saw:


[young Will's first encounter with the Upside Down](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vhFPHYgILN0) .


"I tried to describe it in a way that echoed the language I used for the very first episode of the series, repeating details about Castle Byers and using a phrase, 'petal-like face flaps,' from the Demogorgon's first appearance, to bring the listener back to that time," said Christina Stevens, Audio Description Writer at IDC. "The audience knows so much more about the Upside Down now, but I wanted them to feel the same misty woods, barren trees, and red lightning as the first time we saw it." That same craft shipped in 15 languages, day-and-date, across all three staggered releases of Season 5.


As of 2026, more than 75,000 hours of AD are available on Netflix for members who are blind or low-vision, in more than 50 languages. That’s enough to describe over 40,000 feature-length films, counting each language separately. We’re working to extend that reach, including across our licensed titles. We’re also launching new applications like Originator Studio, an authoring tool built with full screen reader compatibility so blind and low-vision professionals can fully participate in AD workflows.


Workshop for Accessibility in Localization in Taiwan


“I’m proud of this recognition and the pipeline we’re building,” said Elisa Beniero, Netflix's Senior Manager of Content Localization, Strategy and Innovation. “Since 2024, we've supported the


[Audio Description Training Retreats](https://www.adtrainingretreats.com/) , which have graduated nine new AD professionals, including five writers from the 2025 cohort who now work with our partner DVW. This year, we supported a training program for blind narrators and quality-control professionals in Korea, and a curated, hands-on program in Taiwan where industry experts from the disability community taught AD writers and linguists who create Subtitles for the Deaf and Hard of Hearing (SDH). The more we bring blind and low-vision talent directly into these workflows, the better the work gets.”


Thank you to our partners who help every member follow the story, to the community that guides us, and to our members globally for coming along on this journey.
